items.title: Kaimerva: a world around your work
items.summary: A free agent skill and Three.js starter for explorable portfolios. Inspect its design through three original project views.
items.body: This supplied example describes Kaimerva itself. Three authored settings share the same published records and an ordinary HTML reading path. A project or figure can be inspected through an optical iris at sea, a scanner gantry in space, or a glass specimen cabinet in nature. The selected entry and supplied view stay with the reader when its setting changes. Content and supported settings are separate JSON files; new mechanisms still require authored code. These diagrams explain the starter, rather than presenting research results or screenshots.

figure.alt: Three authored portfolio settings connect to one readable collection and content layer.
figure.caption: Original explanatory project diagrams for Kaimerva. These are supplied vector views, not screenshots, publication figures or scientific evidence.

stages.label: Explore the starter
stages.description: Three authored settings share collection destinations and published records. Optional exploration sits beside an HTML reader that opens the work immediately and remains available without WebGL.

stages.label: Inspect the same work
stages.description: The selected entry and supplied view stay shared. The sea iris hinges open, the orbital shutter banks fold and retract, and the woodland cabinet doors swing open. The same source image and explanation remain readable.

stages.label: Edit, then publish
stages.description: Content and supported settings live in separate JSON files and can refresh the local preview. New mechanisms need authored code. Production builds a published-only static snapshot; local saves do not publish the deployed site.

items.title: Inside an interference field
items.summary: An illustrative visual study: place two equal sources, read their radial contributions, then inspect their sum.
items.body: This is original demo artwork, not a paper or a scientific result. Two sources sit at A = (−2.25, 0) and B = (+2.25, 0) in arbitrary coordinates. With k = 2π / 2.4, the final plate evaluates s(x, y) = cos(k rA) + cos(k rB) over x ∈ [−7, 7], y ∈ [−3.5, 3.5], where rA and rB are distances to the sources. Cyan shows positive values, brass negative values, and ink values near zero. The contribution plate shows constant-phase contours of the same two functions. This static scalar analogy does not model physical decay, time evolution, boundary conditions, or calibrated measurements.

figure.alt: Two radial cosine contributions sum into a cyan and brass scalar field. Sources A and B and zero-level contours remain visible.
figure.caption: Original illustrative plates, authored for this starter. The scalar construction is an analogy, not a physical propagation solver, publication figure, or research result.

stages.label: Place the sources
stages.description: A = (−2.25, 0) and B = (+2.25, 0) share one wavelength, 2.4 arbitrary units, and one phase. The source positions remain fixed throughout all three plates.

stages.label: Read each contribution
stages.description: Each contribution is a radial cosine: a = cos(k rA), b = cos(k rB), with k = 2π / 2.4. Solid cyan and brass rings mark positive maxima; dashed rings mark negative minima. These are static constant-phase contours.

stages.label: Inspect their sum
stages.description: The final plate directly samples s = a + b over the same domain. Cyan means positive, brass negative, and dark ink near zero. Thin contours trace 0 and ±1.2. No physical decay, time stepping, or calibration is implied.
